passage:
I'm Sumit. For six weeks last year, I lied every evening at dinner.
I had put my savings, three years of them, into a trading app a friend of a friend swore by. When it froze, a "recovery agent" called and said I could get it back for a fee. I paid that too. Chasing it felt better than admitting it was gone.
At home, Ma asked about my savings once, and I changed the subject so fast she looked at me strangely. I stopped sleeping. I kept refreshing the dead app as if it might wake up.
Wasim noticed first. He cornered me on the office terrace: "You look like someone died." I told him everything and waited for him to call me stupid. He said, "Okay. Today we report it."
We filed complaints on the cybercrime portal and with the regulator that evening. That night I told Ma and Papa. Ma cried. Then she made tea.

qa.q: How long did Sumit lie at dinner?
qa.a: Sumit lied every evening at dinner for six weeks.

qa.q: Why did chasing the loss feel better to Sumit than admitting it?
qa.a: Admitting it meant facing shame and the family's reaction, so paying the recovery fee kept alive a hope that the money wasn't gone.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Telling Wasim everything on the terrace led to reporting that same evening and telling Ma and Papa, which ended the hiding and gave the best chance to limit the damage.

qa.q: What might Ma have felt when she was finally told?
qa.a: Ma likely felt shock and sadness, which is why she cried, but also relief at the truth, shown when she made tea.

grounding: A person who lost savings to a fake scheme hides it out of shame and even pays a recovery fee, until Wasim helps report it and tell the family.

passage:
Branch officer's note, 18 July. Mridul.
Kashish, a customer I know from her salary account, came in asking to break her fixed deposit early, today, in cash. Her hands were shaking and she kept checking her phone.
I asked gently whether everything was all right. After a while she told me: three weeks ago she lost most of her savings in an online investment club. Someone from the club now promised to recover it if she paid a release fee. She had not told her husband. "He'll think I'm an idiot," she said.
I told her the recovery offer is a common second trap, that she is not an idiot, and that reporting early matters.
Outcome today: she decided not to break the deposit. I sat with her while she called the cybercrime helpline and flagged the transactions with our fraud team. She plans to tell her husband tonight, with her sister present.

qa.q: What did Kashish ask to do at the branch?
qa.a: She asked to break her fixed deposit early, today, in cash.

qa.q: What was Kashish afraid of?
qa.a: She was afraid her husband would think she was an idiot, which is why she had hidden the loss.

qa.q: What steps did Mridul take to limit the damage?
qa.a: Mridul explained the recovery offer was a second trap, said she was not an idiot, and sat with her while she called the cybercrime helpline and flagged the transactions with the fraud team.

qa.q: How might Kashish's husband react when told tonight, with her sister present?
qa.a: He may be shocked or upset at first, but hearing it early and with support gives them a better chance to face it together.

grounding: A bank officer notices a woman's distress, learns she hid an investment loss from her husband and is being offered a fake recovery, and helps her report it.

passage:
Pranav hadn't slept properly in two weeks. His ₹4 lakh, five years of savings for a flat, had vanished into a trading app that one morning simply stopped opening.
He hadn't told his wife. Every evening at dinner in their Andheri flat, she talked about the flat they'd see on Sunday, and he nodded, his food like sand.
At night he opened another app, one that promised he could "recover losses" if he deposited a little more. His thumb hovered.
His friend Mridul caught him outside the office, smoking, which he hadn't done in years. "What's going on?"
Pranav told him everything. His voice kept breaking. "She'll never trust me again."
Mridul didn't lecture. "Listen. Chasing it will lose more. Reporting it fast gives the police a chance. And she'd rather hear it from you now than find out later."
That evening Pranav filed a complaint with the cyber police, and the regulator. Then he went home and told his wife.

qa.q: How much had Pranav lost?
qa.a: His ₹4 lakh, five years of savings for a flat.

qa.q: How was Pranav feeling during the two weeks of silence?
qa.a: Pranav felt ashamed and afraid of his wife's reaction, unable to eat or sleep, and tempted to chase the losses.

qa.q: What did Mridul advise, and why did it help?
qa.a: Mridul advised not chasing losses, reporting quickly to the police, and telling his wife, which limits damage and ends the hiding.

qa.q: How might Pranav's wife feel when he tells her?
qa.a: She would likely feel shocked and hurt, but also relieved he told her himself rather than her finding out later.

grounding: It shows an adult who lost savings to a fake scheme hiding it from family out of shame, tempted to chase losses, until a friend helps him report.

passage:
"Jasleen, I need to tell you something. Please sit."
"You're scaring me, Yogesh."
"The investment group. The one I said was doing well. It's gone. The app, the group, all of it."
"Gone? How much?"
"Most of what we'd saved for your sister's wedding contribution." His voice cracked. "I've known for ten days. I didn't tell you. I kept trying to win it back. I lost more."
Jasleen was silent. Then: "Why didn't you tell me?"
"I was ashamed. I thought you'd hate me."
She took a long breath. "I'm angry. Really angry. But I don't hate you. I hate that you carried it alone."
"What do we do?"
"Tonight we write down every transaction. Tomorrow we go to the cyber police together, and we report it to the regulator. And you stop trying to win it back."
Yogesh nodded, tears on his face. "Okay. Together."

qa.q: How long had Yogesh known about the loss before telling Jasleen?
qa.a: Ten days.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh hide the loss?
qa.a: Yogesh felt ashamed and afraid that Jasleen would hate him, so he kept trying to win it back alone.

qa.q: What steps did Jasleen suggest?
qa.a: Writing down every transaction, reporting to the cyber police and the regulator the next day together, and stopping chasing the losses.

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel when Yogesh tells her?
qa.a: Jasleen feels angry, but not hateful, and hurt that he carried it alone.

grounding: It shows an adult who lost savings to a fake scheme hiding it out of shame and chasing losses, then telling his wife and reporting it.

passage:
I'm Mridul, and for two months I hid the worst mistake of my life from my sister Irawati.
We shared a flat. I had put ₹2 lakh, all my savings plus some of our shared emergency fund, into an "AI trading" app a friend recommended. It showed profits every day. Then it froze. Customer support said I had to pay a "release fee" to withdraw.
I paid the fee. Then another. I told myself if I could just get it back, Irawati would never need to know.
Every time she asked why I looked so tired, I said "work." I stopped eating properly. I felt like a fraud in my own home.
One night she found me sitting on the kitchen floor at 3 a.m. She sat down next to me and waited.
I told her everything. She didn't shout. She said, "We report it tomorrow. And no more fees." We went to the cyber police in the morning. I wish I'd told her on day one.

qa.q: What did customer support say Mridul had to pay to withdraw?
qa.a: A "release fee."

qa.q: How was Mridul feeling during the two months of hiding?
qa.a: Mridul felt ashamed and afraid, like a fraud at home, and kept chasing the losses in the hope Irawati would never know.

qa.q: What changed once Mridul told Irawati?
qa.a: Irawati stayed calm, said they would report it and pay no more fees, and they went to the cyber police the next morning.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel finding Mridul on the kitchen floor?
qa.a: Irawati would likely feel worried and concerned, which is why she sat beside Mridul and waited instead of demanding answers.

grounding: An adult recalls hiding investment losses from a sister out of shame and paying more fees to chase them, until telling her and reporting it.

passage:
Counselling note, workplace wellbeing service, Thursday.
Saurabh came in looking exhausted; he said he hasn't slept properly in a week. Three weeks ago he moved most of his savings into an online trading scheme a colleague's friend recommended. The app showed rising profits until he tried to withdraw; now the account is "frozen" unless he pays a "release fee". He hasn't told his wife or parents. He said, "They'll think I'm an idiot," and that part of him wants to pay the fee to get it all back.
I said clearly that he was targeted by people who do this professionally, and that it says nothing about his intelligence. I explained that paying more usually leads to further loss, and that reporting early matters.
Today, with me, he filed a complaint on the national cyber-crime helpline and noted the regulator's complaint route. He agreed to tell his wife tonight, and asked if she could join our next session.
Pema

qa.q: What does the scheme say Saurabh must pay to unlock his account?
qa.a: A release fee.

qa.q: Why has Saurabh kept the loss from his family?
qa.a: Saurabh feels ashamed and afraid, worried that his wife and parents will think he's an idiot.

qa.q: What steps did Pema help Saurabh take?
qa.a: Pema said it said nothing about his intelligence, warned that paying more usually brings further loss, and helped him report to the cyber-crime helpline and note the regulator's route that day.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's wife feel when he tells her tonight?
qa.a: She may feel shocked, hurt and scared at first, but also relieved that he told her and that help is already under way.

grounding: Shows a person who lost savings to a fake scheme feeling shame and fear of the family's reaction and tempted to chase the loss, then reporting early and telling his wife.
